title: Masking meets Supervision: A Strong Learning Alliance

strengths: AugSub provides a simple, technically coherent way to combine supervised learning with stronger regularization through a shared-weight, stop-gradient distillation objective. Its support for dropout, drop-path, and masking makes it practically useful without changing inference.

The ImageNet evidence is substantial. With a fixed 50% masking ratio, AugMask improves all four DeiT-III model sizes by 0.6–0.7 percentage points at 400 epochs and 0.3–0.5 points at 800 epochs (Table 3). Repeated runs in Table A.2 support the central gains.

The improvements are not explained solely by additional computation. Table 6 reports ViT-B accuracy of 84.1% versus 83.7% using 25 versus 26 GPU-days, and MAE ViT-L finetuning improves from 85.5% to 86.1% at the same reported budget.

Evaluation extends across ResNet, Swin, several pretrained representations, robustness benchmarks, and downstream tasks. Particularly persuasive results include ImageNet-A improving from 51.9% to 58.3% for ViT-H and ADE20K gains of 0.4–0.6 mIoU. This breadth and the compute-controlled results support weak acceptance.

Reproducibility is supported by concise pseudocode, detailed training configurations in Appendix B, identified pretrained checkpoints, three-run statistics for several key experiments, and a provided code link.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is incremental relative to existing consistency regularization and self-distillation. Co-sub is explicitly identified as closely related, but there is no direct experimental comparison. The manuscript therefore establishes improvements over conventional training recipes more convincingly than advantages over related sub-model training methods.

The ablations do not isolate the proposed relaxed-target mechanism. Comparing masked-only supervision against AugSub simultaneously introduces a full-image supervised branch and changes the masked branch's target. A shared-weight, two-pass baseline supervised by ground truth on both branches is missing. Furthermore, Figure 3's aggregate gradient norms do not establish the claimed example-wise prioritization: Equation 3 also regularizes confidently misclassified examples. This weakens the explanation, while leaving the implemented objective technically plausible.

The benefit has meaningful boundaries. Section 4.2 acknowledges that CLIP's best-checkpoint accuracy is unchanged, making the reported improvement specific to final-epoch selection. Adding AugMask during transfer finetuning reduces ViT-B CIFAR-100 accuracy from 91.9% to 89.6% (Table 10). These results qualify the claim of a reliably beneficial plug-in across training settings.

Statistical support is uneven. Although the appendix reports repeated runs for selected experiments, small gains such as 0.1 points for BEiT v2 and Swin-T and 0.2 box AP on COCO lack corresponding variability estimates. Several pretraining-only transfer gains are also smaller than the reported standard deviations. Such results should receive less evidential weight than the larger, replicated improvements.
